examGuide.title: Approach the exam question
examGuide.body: Translate a recurrence into an equation for A(x)=sum an xⁿ. Align indices before subtracting series and explicitly keep the initial terms omitted by shifting. Coefficients of products are convolutions. The identity 1/(1−x)^k has coefficient binomial(n+k−1,k−1) and turns many constrained-counting problems into coefficient extraction.

examGuide.title: Worked problem
examGuide.body:
Find the coefficient of x5 in 1/(1−x)³.

**Answer: 21.** Expand using the generalized geometric series: [xⁿ](1−x)⁻³=binomial(n+2,2). At n=5 this is binomial(7,2)=21. Equivalently it counts triples of nonnegative integers with sum 5.

examGuide.title: Conditions and edge cases
examGuide.body:
Ordinary generating functions can be treated as formal series for coefficient identities; a convergence argument is not required for that algebra.

The coefficient of a product is a convolution, not a pointwise multiplication of coefficients.
